title: Workplace Safety & Compliance
author: Safety Training Dept.
description: A comprehensive workplace safety course covering hazard identification, PPE requirements, emergency procedures, and OSHA compliance guidelines.

data.title: Workplace Safety & Compliance
data.body:
Welcome!

This course covers essential workplace safety principles, hazard identification, and compliance requirements. By the end, you will be able to identify common hazards and apply OSHA guidelines.

data.title: Course Overview
data.description: This course contains 7 modules covering hazard identification, PPE, emergency procedures, and compliance requirements.

milestones.title: Emergency Procedures
milestones.description: What to do in an emergency

tabs.title: Physical Hazards
tabs.body: Physical hazards include slippery floors, falling objects, moving machinery, and extreme temperatures. Always be aware of your surroundings.

tabs.title: Chemical Hazards
tabs.body: Chemical hazards include toxic fumes, corrosive substances, and flammable materials. Always read Safety Data Sheets (SDS) before handling.

tabs.title: Ergonomic Hazards
tabs.body: Ergonomic hazards arise from repetitive motions, poor posture, and improper workstation setup. Take regular breaks.

tabs.title: Biological Hazards
tabs.body: Biological hazards include bacteria, viruses, mold, and animal-related risks. Proper hygiene is essential.

hotspots.label: Wet Floor
hotspots.content: This wet floor is a slip hazard. Place a warning sign and mop up immediately.

hotspots.label: Unsecured Shelf
hotspots.content: This heavy shelf is not bolted to the wall. It could topple and cause injury.

hotspots.label: Blocked Exit
hotspots.content: This emergency exit is blocked by boxes. Emergency exits must always remain clear.

hotspots.label: Frayed Wire
hotspots.content: This electrical cord is frayed and could cause a fire or shock. Replace it immediately.

data.title: Hazard Awareness Best Practices
dos: Report hazards immediately to your supervisor
Wear appropriate PPE at all times

panels.title: Head Protection
panels.body: Hard hats protect against falling objects, bumps, and electrical hazards. Choose ANSI-rated helmets appropriate for your work environment.

panels.title: Eye & Face Protection
panels.body: Safety glasses, goggles, and face shields protect against flying debris, chemical splashes, and radiation. Always use ANSI Z87.1 rated eyewear.

panels.title: Hand Protection
panels.body: Select gloves based on the hazard: leather for cuts, nitrile for chemicals, insulated for electricity. Replace when worn or torn.

panels.title: Foot Protection
panels.body: Steel-toed boots protect against falling objects and compression. Anti-slip soles prevent falls on wet surfaces.

panels.title: Respiratory Protection
panels.body: Respirators and masks protect against dust, fumes, and toxic gases. Ensure proper fit testing and filter selection.

steps.title: Sound the Alarm
steps.description: Pull the nearest fire alarm and call 911. Do not attempt to fight the fire unless you are trained and it is small.

steps.title: Evacuate
steps.description: Walk quickly to the nearest exit. Do NOT use elevators. Close doors behind you to slow fire spread.

steps.title: Assembly Point
steps.description: Go to the designated assembly point. Stay at least 50 feet away from the building.

steps.title: Head Count
steps.description: Report to your section warden for a head count. Inform them of any missing persons.

steps.title: Wait for All Clear
steps.description: Do not re-enter the building until the fire department gives the all-clear signal.

data.title: Emergency Decision
data.context: You smell smoke coming from the server room. The smoke alarm has not gone off yet.
data.question: What should you do first?

options.feedback: Risky — you could be exposed to toxic fumes. Let trained personnel handle it.

options.text: Pull the fire alarm and evacuate
options.feedback: Correct! Safety first. Alert everyone and evacuate immediately.

options.text: Wait to see if the alarm goes off automatically
options.feedback: Dangerous — alarms can fail. Act immediately when you detect a hazard.
Too slow for an emergency. Use the fire alarm for immediate response.

questions.question: Which type of PPE protects against airborne particles?
questions.explanation: N95 respirators filter at least 95% of airborne particles.

questions.question: What should you do first when you smell smoke?

options.text: Pull the fire alarm and evacuate

questions.explanation: Always prioritize safety. Pull the alarm and evacuate immediately.

data.title: Workplace Safety Final Assessment
data.instructions: You must score 70% or higher to pass and receive your certificate. You have 3 attempts.

Which agency sets workplace safety standards in the US?

questions.explanation: Never use elevators during a fire. Use stairs.

data.title: Key Takeaways
keyPoints: Workplace hazards fall into physical, chemical, ergonomic, and biological categories
Always select PPE based on the specific hazard and applicable standard
In an emergency: Alarm → Evacuate → Assembly → Head Count → Wait for All Clear
OSHA mandates hearing protection at 85 dB or above
Safety Data Sheets (SDS) provide essential chemical hazard information

title: Customer Service Excellence
author: Learning & Development
description: Master the HEART framework, handle difficult customers with empathy, and elevate your customer service skills.

data.title: Delivering 5-Star Customer Service
data.body:
Welcome!

Great customer service builds loyalty and drives business growth. In this interactive course, you'll learn the HEART framework, handle difficult situations, and practice empathetic communication.

data.title: How much do you know?
data.instructions: Take this quick pre-assessment so we can customize your learning path.

questions.question: What does empathy mean in customer service?

steps.title: Hear
steps.description: Actively listen to the customer. Let them finish speaking without interruption. Use verbal affirmations like "I understand."

steps.title: Empathize
steps.description: Show genuine empathy. Say things like "I can see how frustrating that must be" to validate their feelings.

steps.title: Apologize
steps.description: Offer a sincere apology even if it's not your fault. "I'm sorry you're experiencing this" goes a long way.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.description: Take ownership and find a solution. If you can't fix it immediately, give a clear timeline and follow up.

steps.title: Thank
steps.description: Thank the customer for their patience and for bringing the issue to your attention.

cards.back: "Thank you for sharing that with me. Let me make sure I understand correctly..."
"I completely understand your frustration. That would bother me too."
"I sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. This should not have happened."
"Here's what I'm going to do to fix this for you right away..."
"Thank you for your patience. We really value your feedback."

nodes.text: A customer storms in, visibly upset, and says loudly: "I've been waiting for 30 minutes! This is unacceptable!"

options.text: Respond calmly: "I'm so sorry for the wait. Let me help you right away."
Say: "Everyone has to wait. Please be patient."

nodes.text: The customer calms down slightly. "Well, at least someone is paying attention. My order was wrong last time too."

options.text: "That must have been very frustrating. Let me look into your previous order and fix everything today."
"I'll fix today's order. The previous one is done."

nodes.text: The customer becomes more upset and asks for a manager. You missed an opportunity to de-escalate. Score: 0/20
Your manager resolves the issue. However, you could have handled this yourself using the HEART framework. Score: 5/20
The customer is partially satisfied but feels their past issue was dismissed. Score: 15/20
Excellent! The customer feels heard and valued. They leave happy and tell a friend about the great service. Score: 20/20

title: Introduction to Web Development
author: Tech Academy
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to web development covering HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fundamentals with interactive exercises.

data.title: Learn HTML, CSS & JavaScript
data.body:
Welcome, Future Web Developer!

In this hands-on course you'll build your first web page from scratch. We start with HTML structure, add CSS styling, and bring it to life with JavaScript.

slides.title: What is HTML?
slides.body: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language for creating web pages. It describes the structure of a web page using elements.

slides.title: Elements & Tags
slides.body: HTML elements are defined by a start tag, content, and an end tag: <p>Hello World</p>

slides.title: Document Structure
slides.body: Every HTML page has: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, and <body> elements.

slides.title: Common Elements
slides.body:
• Headings: h1 – h6
  • Paragraphs: p
  • Links: a
  • Images: img
  • Lists: ul, ol, li

cards.back: Main heading — the most important heading on the page. Use only once per page.
Paragraph — defines a block of text content.
Anchor — creates a hyperlink to another page or resource.
Image — embeds an image. Always include alt text for accessibility.
Division — a generic container for grouping elements.
Unordered / Ordered list — contains <li> list items.

data.title: Complete the HTML
data.templateText: To create a link, use the _____ tag with the _____ attribute to specify the URL.

tabs.title: Selectors
tabs.body: CSS selectors target HTML elements. Types include: element (p), class (.intro), id (#header), and attribute ([type="text"]).

tabs.title: Box Model
tabs.body: Every element is a box with: content, padding, border, and margin. Use box-sizing: border-box for predictable sizing.

tabs.title: Flexbox
tabs.body: Flexbox creates flexible layouts. Set display: flex on a container, then use justify-content, align-items, and flex-wrap to control layout.

tabs.title: CSS Grid
tabs.body: Grid creates 2D layouts. Use display: grid with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows to define structure.

data.title: CSS Transformation
data.beforeContent: Plain HTML with no styling — black text on white, no spacing, default fonts, elements stacked vertically.
data.afterContent: Styled page with custom fonts, colors, spacing, responsive layout, shadows, and animations.

events.title: JavaScript Created
events.description: Brendan Eich created JavaScript in 10 days at Netscape.

events.title: Node.js Released
events.description: JavaScript runs on servers with V8 engine.

events.title: ES6 / ES2015
events.description: Major update: let/const, arrow functions, classes, modules.

events.title: Modern JavaScript
events.description: Top programming language with vast ecosystem.

items.label: Variables
items.content: Use let for mutable variables and const for constants. Avoid var.

items.label: Functions
items.content: Functions are declared with function name() {} or const name = () => {} (arrow function).

items.label: DOM Manipulation
items.content: Use document.querySelector() to select elements and modify their content, styles, and attributes.

data.question: Which keyword declares a variable that cannot be reassigned?
data.explanation: const declares a constant — its value cannot be reassigned after initialization.

data.title: What You Learned
keyPoints: HTML provides the structure of web pages using elements and tags
CSS controls visual presentation: colors, layout, typography
JavaScript adds interactivity and dynamic behavior
The Box Model, Flexbox, and Grid are key CSS layout tools
Modern JavaScript (ES6+) uses let/const, arrow functions, and modules
data.nextSteps: Build a personal portfolio page to practice everything you've learned!
